**Saturday, June 23, 1956**

You arrived on a Saturday in the middle of a year that was quietly remaking the world. Dwight Eisenhower was in the White House. The Korean War had been over for three years, but the Cold War was deepening in new ways — Stalin had died in 1953, and his successor Nikita Khrushchev had just delivered his "Secret Speech" four months earlier, denouncing Stalin's crimes to a stunned Communist Party audience. The thaw after Stalin was real, but so was the terror. No one knew quite what came next.

---

**The birthday you share**

Alan Turing was born on June 23, 1912 — exactly forty-four years before you. He is, by most accounts, the person most responsible for the theoretical foundations of computing: the concept of the universal machine, the formalization of what an algorithm is, the breaking of the Enigma cipher that shortened the Second World War. He was also prosecuted by the British government in 1952 for homosexuality, chemically castrated as a condition of avoiding prison, and died in June 1954 — two years before you were born, on what would have been his forty-second birthday.

You arrived into a world still largely innocent of what Turing had set in motion. The computers of 1956 were room-sized machines operated by specialists, inaccessible to ordinary life. Over the seventy years that followed, his foundational ideas — refined, extended, and eventually miniaturized — would become the infrastructure of everything. You have now lived into the age of artificial intelligence, the direct descendant of the theoretical work Turing did before most people understood why it mattered. He didn't live to see any of it. You've seen nearly all of it.

---

**Six days after you were born**

On June 29, 1956 — when you were less than a week old — President Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act into law. It authorized 41,000 miles of interstate highway and the largest public works project in American history up to that point. Eisenhower had been convinced of the military necessity of rapid cross-country movement partly by his experience watching German Autobahns during WWII, but the civilian transformation was far greater than the military one. The Interstate System reshaped where Americans lived, how they shopped, which cities grew and which shrank, and what the country looked like from above. The suburban sprawl, the road trip, the trucking industry, the American relationship to the automobile — all of it was amplified by that legislation. You were six days old when the physical America you would grow up in was essentially signed into existence.

---

**Your sixteenth birthday**

On June 23, 1972 — the day you turned sixteen — President Nixon signed Title IX of the Education Amendments into law. The text was spare: no person shall be excluded from participation in, or denied the benefits of, any education program receiving federal funding on the basis of sex. Twelve words that transformed American schools, universities, and athletic programs over the decades that followed. Girls' sports programs that barely existed would become fully funded. Professional schools that quietly capped women's enrollment would open. The generation of women entering college in the late 1970s and 1980s entered a different institution than the one their mothers had found. It happened on your birthday.

---

**The world you entered**

The summer of 1956 was electric with things that hadn't quite happened yet. Elvis Presley had recorded "Heartbreak Hotel" in January and watched it go to number one; he would appear on The Ed Sullivan Show that September, seen by sixty million people. Rock and roll existed, but its full force was still arriving. Television had reached about three-quarters of American homes, but the content was still tentative — Milton Berle, variety shows, early sitcoms. The medium was learning what it was.

In the South, the Montgomery Bus Boycott — begun the previous December after Rosa Parks' arrest — was still ongoing. The Supreme Court had ruled school segregation unconstitutional in Brown v. Board of Education two years earlier, but the ruling was being resisted with massive force across the region. The civil rights movement was building toward its most dramatic decade, and the country you were born into was still a legally segregated one in ways that would seem unimaginable to Americans born later.

---

**The arc**

You are 70 years old now. You were born before the Sputnik launch, before the first American in space, before the birth control pill was approved, before the Beatles existed. You were thirteen when humans walked on the Moon. You were thirty-three when the Berlin Wall fell. You were forty-five on September 11, 2001.

The computers that occupied whole buildings the year you were born now fit in a pocket and carry more processing power than existed on Earth in 1956. The highways laid down the week after your birth became the circulatory system of a continent. The law signed on your sixteenth birthday changed who could become a doctor, a lawyer, an engineer, an Olympic athlete.

Alan Turing never lived to see the world his ideas built. You have watched nearly the whole construction — from the first transistor radios to the large language models that can now discuss his legacy in conversational prose. That is an extraordinary seventy years to have inhabited.
